rationale: A wins because it finds the extra usable user-side story without inventing a fairy tale: “What happens when Bumble's AI writes your opening line” is a real hands-on product test, not a padded duplicate. B is clean and disciplined, but it stops at three shapes and leaves that reviewable product experience on the floor while only refusing “Bumble user finds love through AI matchmaking.” Both are above the usual AI pitch sludge; A is just more useful to a founder choosing where to aim first.
gaps_in_A: “it is the first product the returned founder has put their name on” is stronger than the supplied facts. The update says the relaunch is under the returning founder-CEO, not that it is their first product or first big move.
“Bumble sells subscriptions” is probably true, but the supplied facts only say paying users. In a blind grounded exercise, that should be phrased as paying-user economics unless filings are supplied.
“Story type: customer-story” is mislabeled for “What happens when Bumble's AI writes your opening line.” This is a hands-on product test, not a customer story with a named user or outcome.
gaps_in_B: It misses the legitimate hands-on review angle. Refusing “Bumble user finds love through AI matchmaking” is correct, but the usable version is testing match suggestions and AI openers without claiming romantic success.
“Bumble's entire brand is a single authentic human gesture” overstates the supplied fact. The facts say women-message-first remains core; “entire brand” is a columnist flourish, not evidence.

“the user criticism of AI-assisted dating gives the tension a current voice” assumes freshness and scale the update does not provide. The set later asks for that proof, but the angle copy still leans on it.

“Two of the three angles are thin without direct quotes” is too broad. The markets angle needs numbers and reporting dates more than quotes; the founder angle is the one that truly dies without founder access.
